name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,319

entries.clue: Drink tea with right university person? Indeed! (10)

blocks.note: cha is slang for tea
R = right
a don is a university teacher
nay in its old sense of 'indeed, what is more'

annotation.surface: Someone takes tea with a well-connected academic and is suitably impressed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drink tea' reads as a verb and its object, but Drink is the definition and tea starts the wordplay. NAY here is the emphatic 'and more than that', not 'no'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one particular white wine, and a wine is one kind of drink.

entries.clue: Important official translation of icon’s memoirs (12)

indicatorNotes.translation of: translating turns the letters into a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters including the S of the possessive

annotation.surface: A celebrity's autobiography is being translated for a foreign edition.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S counts as a letter of the fodder, which is easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A commissioner is a senior official in charge of a department or body.

entries.clue: Included as part of exam on genetics (5)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Included' works as 'among' in the sense 'counted in with': 'included were ...' / 'among them were ...'

indicatorNotes.as part of: the answer is literally part of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run from the third letter of exam, through on, to the first letter of genetics

annotation.surface: A student notes which topics appear on a genetics exam.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans three words: ex(AM ON G)enetics.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose preposition-for-participle swap: 'the items included were...' and 'among the items were...' say the same thing.

entries.clue: Diddle English female (3)

blocks.note: to do someone is to cheat them
E = English

annotation.surface: An Englishwoman is being swindled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'English female' reads as one phrase, but English only supplies E; female alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the word names the female of deer, rabbits and hares, so 'female' is a broad stand-in.

entries.clue: Tortilla chips, exotic nosh a Conservative tucks into (6)

indicatorNotes.exotic: exotic suggests something strange, so rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.tucks into: C goes inside the rearranged letters as food is tucked in

blocks.note: NOSH A rearranged
C = Conservative, placed after NA

annotation.surface: A Tory politician digs into some foreign snack food.
annotation.walkthrough: Nosh is informal for food. The Conservative is only the letter C, dropped into NA_HOS.
annotation.definitionFit: Nachos are fried tortilla chips, usually topped with cheese.

entries.clue: Strangely use mag repeatedly — activity that should be avoided (1,4,4)

indicatorNotes.repeatedly: doing something repeatedly means doing it more than once, so the word before it is written twice

blocks.note: USE plus MAG twice, anagram fodder of 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone warns against reading the same magazine over and over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Use' reads as the verb of the instruction, but it is fodder; only 'repeatedly' tells you to double MAG.
annotation.definitionFit: A mug's game is a pursuit only a fool would take on.

entries.clue: Minimal cover? Two-wheeler, not fully insured — not ideal at first (6)

indicatorNotes.not fully: BIKE is cut short by its last letter
indicatorNotes.at first: take the opening letters of the next three words

blocks.note: BIKE without its last letter
I-nsured N-ot I-deal

annotation.surface: A cyclist grumbles about having only minimal insurance on a bike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minimal cover' looks like part of the insurance story; the question mark flags that it is a swimsuit. 'Not fully' seems to go with 'insured', but it trims the bike.
annotation.definitionFit: A bikini covers about as little as clothing can.

entries.clue: One breaking rules errs — art songs need rewriting (12)

indicatorNotes.need rewriting: the letters are to be written out again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A composer admits a mistake and says the art songs need rewriting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Errs' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A transgressor is someone who breaks a law or rule.

entries.clue: Get right away from ill-tempered animal (5)

indicatorNotes.Get right away from: take R (right) away from the next word

blocks.note: morose = sullen
R = right, removed

annotation.surface: Advice to keep well clear of a bad-tempered beast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get right away' reads as 'flee completely'; here right is R, taken out of MOROSE.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is the largest species of deer, and 'animal' is the broad class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Old news announcer welcoming Open University messenger (7)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: CRIER takes OU in, as a host welcomes a guest

blocks.note: a town crier called out the news
the initial letters of Open University, the UK distance-learning university

annotation.surface: A veteran broadcaster greets a delivery from the Open University.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old news announcer' suggests a retired broadcaster, but it is a town crier, who shouted public announcements in the street.
annotation.definitionFit: A courier carries messages or parcels.

entries.clue: Cleverly innovative, one using idea at the outset differently (9)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: take the first letter of idea

blocks.note: anagram fodder
first letter of idea, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A description of an inventor who approaches ideas in an original way.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'one using' plus the I from idea; the whole surface reads as praise, hiding the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Ingenious means clever and original in design.

entries.clue: Means of identifying someone in call beginning to play dead (9)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: take the first letter of play

blocks.note: to call someone something is to name them
first letter of play
the late X = the dead X

annotation.surface: Someone on a phone call is told to play dead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link here, not a container instruction: the pieces simply follow each other.
annotation.definitionFit: A nameplate on a door or desk shows who is there.

entries.clue: Somewhere to stay initially is needed now (3)

indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so only the start of each word is used

blocks.note: I-s N-eeded N-ow

annotation.surface: A traveller urgently needs a place to stay.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one plea; 'initially' sits between definition and fodder and belongs to the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An inn offers rooms for travellers.

entries.clue: Dishonest scheme interrupted by resistance — get out fast! (5)

indicatorNotes.interrupted by: R breaks into the middle of SCAM

blocks.note: a scam is a swindle
R = resistance in physics

annotation.surface: A fraud meets resistance, and the crook shouts to the gang to flee.
annotation.walkthrough: R for resistance comes from physics, where it is the symbol in Ohm's law.
annotation.definitionFit: Scram! is a slangy order to leave at once.

entries.clue: Keep in mind tips from expert in wet weather (6)

indicatorNotes.tips from: the tips of a word are its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.in: 'tips from expert in wet weather' puts the tips inside the weather, as a person is in the rain

blocks.note: rain is wet weather
E-xper-T, placed inside RAIN

annotation.surface: Someone reminds themselves of an expert's advice for rainy days.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like advice; it means the end letters of expert.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the memory sense: facts you keep hold of are ones you keep in mind.

entries.clue: Getting rid of levying money for Government? No opening for that! (5)

indicatorNotes.No opening for that!: 'that' points back to the word just clued, and giving it no opening means its first letter goes

blocks.note: taxing = levying money for the state; T removed

annotation.surface: A protester rejects a new tax outright.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No opening for that!' sounds like a flat refusal; it tells you to drop the T of TAXING.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative synonym: taking an axe to jobs or schemes is headline slang for scrapping them.

entries.clue: Maybe split second’s importance (6)

blocks.note: 'maybe' marks a split second as one example of a brief instant
the older sense of weight or significance, as in 'of great ...'

annotation.surface: A remark on how much can turn on a single instant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks the split second as an example of a moment. The less common sense, moment = importance, lives on in 'momentous'.
annotation.definitionFit: A moment is a brief time, and also weight or significance.

entries.clue: Not permitted in public (3)

blocks.note: banned or off the table, as in 'smoking indoors is ...'
known to everyone, as in 'the secret is ...'

annotation.surface: A rule banning something in public places.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as one rule, but it splits into two separate meanings of OUT.
annotation.definitionFit: Out means both ruled out and out in the open.

entries.clue: Out of order, moped near walking area (9)

indicatorNotes.Out of order: the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone complains about a scooter parked by a pedestrian area.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' reads as a complaint about bad behaviour; it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A promenade is a paved walkway, often along a seafront.

entries.clue: Guardian’s fury as side finally changes (5)

indicatorNotes.side finally changes: the last letter, R (right, a side), becomes L (left, the other side)

blocks.note: anger = fury
the final R (right) switches to L (left)

annotation.surface: A newspaper reports rising fury as a team changes sides.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guardian’s' reads as the newspaper's; the ’s is 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay. Right and left are the two sides.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: from 'guardian angel', the spirit believed to watch over each person, so either word can stand for the other.

entries.clue: Regularly visited, seems I have high opinion of country! (7)

indicatorNotes.Regularly visited: only every other letter is called on

blocks.note: s-E-e-M-s-I: every second letter
to rate someone is to think highly of them

annotation.surface: A tourist, having visited often, declares admiration for the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly visited' sounds like a travel habit; it picks alternate letters of 'seems I'.
annotation.definitionFit: An emirate is a state ruled by an emir, such as Qatar or Kuwait.

entries.clue: Spurious attempt to return on board bus (5)

indicatorNotes.to return: to return is to go back, so the word is read back to front
indicatorNotes.on board: OG gets on board, inside BUS

blocks.note: have a go = make an attempt
holds OG between B and US

annotation.surface: A passenger makes a feeble attempt to get back on a bus.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spurious attempt' reads as one phrase, but Spurious alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe something false passed off as genuine.

entries.clue: See you later in Derby? Excellent! (3)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits in the next words

blocks.note: the last two letters of Derby and the first of Excellent

annotation.surface: Someone asks if they will meet in Derby, a city in the English Midlands.
annotation.walkthrough: Der(BY E)xcellent: the question mark splits the hidden letters across a break in the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Bye is a casual farewell, like see you later.

entries.clue: Irish footballer George by wine store, it’s said, in book bought by many (10)

indicatorNotes.it’s said: the word is spoken, so only its sound counts

blocks.note: George Best, the Northern Irish Manchester United winger
a cellar stores wine

annotation.surface: A biography of footballer George Best, famous for his drinking, is a big hit.
annotation.walkthrough: George Best was a 1960s Manchester United star whose heavy drinking was notorious, which makes the wine store fit the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A bestseller is a book that sells in large numbers.
